title: Computer System and Performance
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 1 combines foundational computer architecture theory (44%, 22 questions per 50-Q test) with quantitative performance analysis, clock/cycle calculations, CPI/MIPS metrics, pipeline timing, and Amdahl's Law problems (56%, 28 questions per 50-Q test).
learningObjectives: Distinguish between Computer Architecture (logical/programmer view) and Computer Organization (physical/hardware implementation).
Identify the four main functions and four structural components of a single-processor and multicore computer system.
Map the 7-level Computer Level Hierarchy from Digital Logic (Level 0) to User Level (Level 6) and contrast Von Neumann vs. Harvard architectures.
Trace the evolution of computers (Generations 0–4) and Intel processor families, applying Moore's Law.
Calculate clock period, frequency, CPU execution time, weighted average CPI, MIPS, pipeline execution cycles, and Amdahl's Law speedups.
Compare CISC vs. RISC design philosophies (including register windows and instruction cycle counts) and classify parallel systems using Flynn's Taxonomy.

formulas.name: Clock Cycle Time & Frequency
formulas.formula: T_cycle = 1 / f_clock

formulas.name: Relative Performance
formulas.formula: P_A / P_B = Execution_Time_B / Execution_Time_A = k

formulas.name: CPU Execution Time
formulas.formula: CPU Time = Clock Cycles * Cycle Time = (IC * CPI) / Clock Rate

formulas.name: Weighted Average CPI
formulas.formula: CPI = Sum(CPI_i * IC_i) / Total_IC = Sum(CPI_i * Relative_Freq_i)

formulas.name: MIPS (Millions of Instructions/Sec)
formulas.formula: MIPS = IC / (Execution_Time * 10^6) = Clock_Rate / (CPI * 10^6)

misconceptions: Confusing powers of 10 (10^3, 10^6, 10^9 used for clock rates and communication bandwidth) with powers of 2 (2^10=1024, 2^20, 2^30 used for binary memory capacity).
Assuming a higher clock frequency (GHz) or higher MIPS rating always guarantees faster program execution without accounting for Instruction Count (IC) and CPI.
Applying Amdahl's Law as S = (1-f) + f*k instead of taking the reciprocal of the new normalized execution time: S = 1 / ((1-f) + f/k).
Confusing Computer Architecture (ISA, addressing modes, data types) with Computer Organization (control signals, circuit design, memory technology).

title: Top Level View of Computer Function
classification: Mixed (50% Theory / 50% Practical Tracing & Bus/Interrupt Calculations)
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 2 balances architectural concepts of instruction cycles, interrupts, DMA, and bus design (50%, 25 questions per 50-Q test) with practical hex machine-code execution traces, Interrupt Vector Table address calculations, I/O vs. memory addressing, and bus capacity/bandwidth calculations (50%, 25 questions per 50-Q test).
learningObjectives: Explain the three key concepts of the Von Neumann architecture and identify the top-level components of a computer system.
Describe the roles of CPU internal registers (PC, IR, MAR, MBR, I/O AR, I/O BR, AC, PSW flags) during instruction fetch and execution.
Trace hexadecimal machine code execution step-by-step across memory and CPU registers (PC, AC, IR) and map the Instruction Cycle State Diagram.
Classify interrupts (Program, Timer, I/O, Hardware Failure, Software INT n), compare polling vs. interrupt-driven I/O, and resolve nested multiple interrupts.
Calculate x86 Interrupt Vector Table (IVT) ISR pointer addresses and compare Separate (Isolated) I/O vs. Memory-Mapped I/O.
Analyze system bus structures (Data, Address, Control lines), bus arbitration/timing (Synchronous vs. Asynchronous), and calculate maximum addressable memory from address bus widths.

formulas.name: x86 Interrupt Vector Table ISR Address
formulas.formula: Vector_Address = n * 4 (4 bytes per entry: 2-byte Offset + 2-byte Segment)

formulas.name: IVT Total Size
formulas.formula: Total_Size = 256 vectors * 4 bytes/vector = 1024 bytes = 1 KB

formulas.name: Maximum Addressable Memory Locations
formulas.formula: Max_Locations = 2^n (where n = Address Bus width in bits)

formulas.name: Hex Machine Instruction Format (Figure 3.5)
formulas.formula: 16-bit word = 4-bit Opcode (1 hex digit) + 12-bit Address (3 hex digits)

misconceptions: Confusing MAR (Memory Address Register, connected to address bus lines) with MBR (Memory Buffer Register, connected to data bus lines).
Assuming software interrupts (like x86 INT n) are asynchronous hardware signals rather than synchronous machine instructions.
Forgetting that when handling multiple interrupts via priorities, a higher-priority interrupt preempts a lower-priority ISR, which later resumes after the higher-priority ISR finishes.
Confusing the role of Address Bus width (which determines maximum addressable memory capacity 2^n) with Data Bus width (which determines how many bits are transferred in parallel per bus cycle).

title: Computer Memory: Cache, Internal & External Storage
classification: Mixed — Problem-Heavy (36% Theory / 64% Practical Calculations & Traces)
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 3 spans two comprehensive slide decks with intensive practical problem-solving (64%, 32 questions per 50-Q test) including Direct/Associative/Set-Associative cache address bit partitioning, cache simulation traces, LRU/LFU replacement traces, Big/Little-Endian memory layouts, DRAM pin multiplexing, memory interleaving, disk capacity/access-time equations, and RAID capacity/fault-tolerance analysis, paired with core memory hierarchy theory (36%, 18 questions per 50-Q test).
learningObjectives: Characterize memory systems by location, capacity, unit of transfer, access method (Sequential, Direct, Random, Associative), and the Memory Hierarchy Pyramid.
Compare SRAM vs. DRAM cell structures, volatility, refresh requirements, and ROM technologies (MROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash).
Determine byte ordering in memory under Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian conventions and analyze DRAM 2D matrix organization (RAS/CAS multiplexing) and Memory Interleaving.
Calculate Tag, Line/Set, and Word offset bit fields and decompose hexadecimal addresses for Direct Mapping, Fully Associative Mapping, and k-Way Set-Associative Mapping.
Simulate 2-Way Set-Associative cache read traces, execute LRU and LFU page replacement algorithms, and contrast Write-Through vs. Write-Back policies and multicore cache coherency.
Calculate magnetic disk storage capacity and total disk access time (Seek + Rotational Latency + Transfer), and evaluate SSD architecture, RAID Levels 0–6, and CD-ROM/DVD optical formats.

formulas.name: Direct Mapping Address Partition
formulas.formula: Address = (s + w) bits; Block size = 2^w; Cache lines m = 2^r; Line i = j mod m; Tag = (s - r) bits, Line = r bits, Word = w bits

formulas.name: Fully Associative Address Partition
formulas.formula: Address = (s + w) bits; Tag = s bits; Word = w bits

formulas.name: k-Way Set-Associative Address Partition
formulas.formula: Cache lines m = v * k; Sets v = 2^d; Set i = j mod v; Tag = (s - d) bits, Set = d bits, Word = w bits

formulas.name: Low-Order Cyclic Memory Interleaving
formulas.formula: Bank b = A mod B; Word_in_Bank w = A div B

formulas.name: Magnetic Disk Capacity
formulas.formula: Capacity = (bytes/sector) * (avg sectors/track) * (tracks/surface) * (surfaces/platter) * (platters/disk)

formulas.name: Magnetic Disk Access Time
formulas.formula: T_access = T_seek + T_rotation + T_transfer; T_rot = 0.5 * (60/R) * 1000 ms; T_trans = (60/R) * (1/sectors_per_track) * 1000 ms

misconceptions: Confusing the number of cache lines m = 2^r (used in Direct Mapping) with the number of cache sets v = 2^d = m / k (used in k-Way Set-Associative Mapping): in 2-way set associative on the same cache size, d = r - 1 and the Tag field grows by 1 bit!
Reversing Big-Endian (most significant byte at lowest memory address) and Little-Endian (least significant byte at lowest memory address, used in x86).
Using full rotation time (60/R) instead of average half-rotation time (0.5 * 60 / R) when calculating average rotational latency for a magnetic disk.
Assuming RAID 5 requires exactly 5 disks (Slide 86 explicitly warns: 'N.B. DOES NOT MEAN 5 DISKS!!!!!') or confusing RAID 0 (striping with zero fault tolerance) with RAID 1 (mirroring).

title: The Central Processing Unit (CPU)
classification: Mixed (44% Theory / 56% Practical Addressing, Register & Flag Problems)
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 4 combines CPU organization and Intel microprocessor evolution theory (44%, 22 questions per 50-Q test) with hands-on practical exercises in x86 Real-Mode 20-bit physical address calculation, segment overlap aliasing, sub-register aliasing (RAX/EAX/AX/AH/AL), EFLAGS/RFLAGS bit evaluation, and Protected Mode descriptor/paging translation (56%, 28 questions per 50-Q test).
learningObjectives: Explain the internal structure of the CPU (ALU with shifter, complementer, status flags, Control Unit, Register File, Internal CPU Bus) and the four CPU functions (Fetch, Decode, Execute, Store).
Distinguish between User-Visible Registers (General Purpose, Data, Address, Condition Codes) and Control & Status Registers (PC, IR, MAR, MBR).
Trace the architectural evolution of Intel x86 processors from the 16-bit 8086/8088 through the 80286, 32-bit 80386 (IA-32), P6 family, Pentium 4/Xeon, Pentium-M, EM64T, and 64-bit x64 (IA-32e mode).

Identify the specialized roles and sub-register aliasing of IA-32 and x86-64 General-Purpose Registers (RAX/EAX/AX/AH/AL, RCX, RDX, RBX, RSP, RBP, RSI, RDI, R8–R15), Segment Registers, FPU/MMX/XMM registers, and EIP/RIP.
Evaluate Status Flags (CF, PF, AF, ZF, SF, OF), Control Flags (DF), and System Flags (TF, IF, IOPL, NT, RF, VM) in the EFLAGS/RFLAGS register.

Calculate 20-bit linear (physical) addresses from `Segment:Offset` logical addresses in Real-Address Mode, analyze segment overlap, and trace Protected Mode logical-to-linear-to-physical translation via GDT/LDT and 4 KB Paging.

formulas.name: Real-Mode 20-Bit Physical Address
formulas.formula: Physical_Address = (Segment_Hex * 10h) + Offset_Hex = (Segment << 4) + Offset

formulas.name: Segment Overlap Aliasing
formulas.formula: Seg_1 * 10h + Off_1 = Seg_2 * 10h + Off_2  =>  Off_2 = Off_1 - (Seg_2 - Seg_1) * 10h

formulas.name: Protected Mode Linear Address
formulas.formula: Linear_Address (32-bit) = Descriptor_Base_Address (32-bit) + Offset (32-bit)

formulas.name: Parity Flag (PF) Rule
formulas.formula: PF = 1 if count_of_1_bits(Result[7:0]) mod 2 == 0 (even parity in least-significant byte), else 0

misconceptions: Adding Segment + Offset directly as 16-bit numbers instead of shifting the 16-bit Segment left by 4 bits (multiplying by 10h = 16 decimal) before adding the 16-bit Offset in Real-Address Mode.

Assuming 32-bit index/pointer registers (ESI, EDI, EBP, ESP) have 8-bit high/low sub-registers like AH/AL in 32-bit IA-32 mode (Slide 3.22 explicitly notes ESI, EDI, EBP, ESP have only 16-bit names SI, DI, BP, SP in 32-bit mode, whereas x86-64 later added SIL, DIL, BPL, SPL).
Confusing the Carry Flag (CF, which indicates unsigned arithmetic overflow/borrow) with the Overflow Flag (OF, which indicates signed two's complement overflow).
Assuming each 64 KB segment in Real-Address Mode is disjoint: in fact, a new segment starts every 10h (16) bytes, so segments overlap heavily and logical addresses are not unique.

title: Data Representation and Computer Arithmetic
classification: Problem-Intensive (26% Theory / 74% Practical Conversions & Binary/BCD/IEEE-754 Arithmetic)
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 5 is heavily quantitative and problem-driven (74%, 37 questions per 50-Q test), featuring integer and fractional radix conversions (Binary, Octal, Decimal, Hex), unsigned binary arithmetic, Sign-Magnitude, 1's and 2's Complement arithmetic, BCD addition with +6 correction, and IEEE 754 (32-bit/64-bit/8-bit) floating-point conversions, paired with foundational representation rules (26%, 13 questions per 50-Q test).
learningObjectives: Convert integers and fractional numbers accurately between Binary (base 2), Octal (base 8), Decimal (base 10), and Hexadecimal (base 16).
Perform unsigned binary addition (including fractional binary numbers), subtraction with borrow, and multiplication.

Represent signed integers in Sign-Magnitude, One's Complement, and Two's Complement formats, and execute signed addition/subtraction (including end-around carry in 1's complement and carry discard in 2's complement).

Encode decimal numbers in Unpacked and Packed BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal), identify forbidden 4-bit nibbles (1010–1111), and perform multi-digit BCD addition using the +6 (0110_2) decade correction rule.

Decode and encode real numbers in IEEE 754 Single Precision (32-bit, bias 127), Double Precision (64-bit, bias 1023), and the slide deck's 8-bit Floating-Point format (1-bit sign, 3-bit exponent with bias 3, 4-bit mantissa), and identify special encodings (±0, ±∞, NaN).

formulas.name: Positional Radix Value
formulas.formula: Value = Sum_{i=-m}^{n-1} d_i * R^i

formulas.name: Two's Complement Negation
formulas.formula: Twos_Comp(A) = Ones_Comp(A) + 1 = (~A) + 1

formulas.name: BCD Addition Decade Correction
formulas.formula: If 4-bit Decade_Sum > 9 or Carry_Out == 1: Decade_Corrected = Decade_Sum + 0110_2 (+6)

formulas.name: IEEE 754 Single Precision (32-bit)
formulas.formula: X = (-1)^S * (1.m) * 2^(e - 127)  [1-bit S, 8-bit e = E + 127, 23-bit fraction m]

formulas.name: Slide 8-Bit Floating-Point Format
formulas.formula: [1-bit Sign | 3-bit Exponent (bias = 3) | 4-bit Mantissa fraction after 1.]

misconceptions: When converting a decimal fraction to binary/hex/octal by repeated multiplication, reading the integer parts from bottom-to-top instead of top-to-bottom (integers use division and read bottom-to-top; fractions use multiplication and read top-to-bottom!).

In One's Complement addition of negative numbers, forgetting to add the end-around carry out of the MSB back into the LSB (Slide 4.28), whereas in Two's Complement addition the carry out of the MSB is discarded (Slide 4.29).

In BCD addition, forgetting to add 0110_2 (6) to a 4-bit decade when the binary sum produces a carry out to the next decade even if the 4-bit nibble itself is <= 9 (e.g., 8 + 9 = 17 = 1_0001_2 requires +0110_2 -> 0001_0111_BCD = 17, Slide 4.34).
Including the implicit leading '1' before the binary point inside the 23-bit mantissa field m of a normalized IEEE 754 floating-point number (only the fractional bits after '1.' are stored in m).

title: x86/x86-64 Assembly Language & CPU Instruction Set
classification: Code-Tracing & Practical-Heavy (30% Theory / 70% Practical Assembly Tracing & Addressing)
recommendedDistributionNote: Chapter 6 combines two lecture decks on NASM assembly programming and the x86/x86-64 instruction set. Because exams heavily test code execution tracing, register/flag states, effective address calculation, bitwise masking, and MUL/IMUL/DIV/IDIV register pairs, 70% (35 questions per 50-Q test) are practical assembly-tracing and calculation problems and 30% (15 questions per 50-Q test) test assembler structure, directives, and instruction semantics.
learningObjectives: Apply bitwise masking idioms (AND to clear/isolate bits, OR to set bits, XOR to toggle/invert bits, SHL/SHR/SAR/ROL/ROR to shift/rotate bits).
Explain the role of an assembler (NASM, MASM, GAS, FASM, TASM), execute the Linux 64-bit (`elf64`) and 32-bit (`elf_i386`) NASM/LD build pipeline, and structure `.data`, `.bss`, and `.text` sections.
Calculate memory allocation sizes and initial byte values for NASM `DX` (`db, dw, dd, dq, dt`), `times`, and `RESX` (`resb, resw`) directives.
Identify Register, Immediate, Direct, and x86 Scaled-Index Indirect addressing modes and compute effective addresses `Addr = Base + (Index * Scale) + Displacement`.
Trace data transfer (`MOV, MOVZX, MOVSX, XCHG, LEA, PUSH, POP`) and arithmetic (`ADD, SUB, INC, DEC, NEG, CMP`) instructions and determine exact register values and `CF, ZF, SF, OF` status flags.
Trace conditional branching (`JE/JZ, JNE/JNZ, JG/JL, JGE/JLE, JA/JB`), procedure calls (`CALL/RET`), and counter loops (`LOOP` with `RCX/ECX`).
Trace 8-bit, 16-bit, and 32-bit unsigned/signed multiplication and division (`MUL, IMUL` [1, 2, and 3 operands], `DIV, IDIV`) across implicit register pairs (`AX`, `DX:AX`, `EDX:EAX`, `AL/AH`).

formulas.name: x86 Scaled-Index Effective Address
formulas.formula: Addr(ind) = Base + (Index * Scale) + Disp

formulas.name: Bitwise Mask Idioms (Bit k, 0-indexed)
formulas.formula: Set bit k: x | (1<<k); Clear bit k: x & ~(1<<k); Toggle bit k: x ^ (1<<k); Keep low 4 bits: x & 0x0F

formulas.name: MUL / IMUL Destination Register Pairs
formulas.formula: 8-bit: AL * src8 -> AX; 16-bit: AX * src16 -> DX:AX; 32-bit: EAX * src32 -> EDX:EAX

formulas.name: DIV / IDIV Dividend, Quotient & Remainder
formulas.formula: 8-bit: AX / src8 -> AL (Quot), AH (Rem); 16-bit: DX:AX / src16 -> AX (Quot), DX (Rem); 32-bit: EDX:EAX / src32 -> EAX (Quot), EDX (Rem)

misconceptions: Assuming `INC` and `DEC` update all arithmetic status flags: Slide 6.54 explicitly notes that `INC` (and `DEC`) updates relevant arithmetic flags (ZF, SF, OF, AF, PF) but DOES NOT modify the Carry Flag (`CF`)!

Confusing `MOVZX` (zero-extension, filling upper bits with 0s regardless of sign) with `MOVSX` (sign-extension, replicating the sign bit MSB into upper bits, so `0FFh` becomes `FFFFFFFFh`, Slide 22 of `ch06_part1_2.pdf`).
Confusing `LEA reg, [addr]` (which loads the effective address `addr` itself into `reg` without dereferencing memory) with `MOV reg, [addr]` (which loads the memory contents at `addr` into `reg`).

Forgetting to clear `DX` (`mov dx, 0`) or `EDX` (`xor edx, edx`) before executing a 16-bit or 32-bit unsigned `DIV` instruction, since `DIV` divides the full 32-bit `DX:AX` or 64-bit `EDX:EAX` dividend!
